title: Pratap Singh: The King of Many Names
body: Susengpha succeeded his father as Ahom king. As he was already advanced in years when he became king, he was nicknamed the Burha Raja. He was also called Buddha Svarga Narayan for his great wisdom, and Pratap Singh because of the great deeds done during his reign. Pratap Singh is the name by which he is best known.
key_facts: Ahom name: Susengpha
Nicknamed Burha Raja because he was old when crowned
Called Buddha Svarga Narayan for his wisdom
Best known as Pratap Singh
image_query: Elderly Ahom king crowned in a wooden palace hall
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 106

title: The Jaintia Princess and the Kachari War (1606)
body: Jasa Manik, Raja of Jaintia, who was on bad terms with the Kachari king Pratap Narayan, offered his daughter to Pratap Singh on condition that she was fetched through Kachari country. The Kachari king refused passage and raided an Ahom village. In June 1606 Pratap Singh sent troops up the Kallang and Kopili, defeated the Kacharis at Dharamtika, and in November the princess was escorted from Jaintiapur to Raha.
key_facts: Jaintia Raja Jasa Manik tried to embroil the Ahoms with the Kacharis
Kachari Raja Pratap Narayan refused passage
Ahom campaign began in June 1606
Kacharis defeated at Dharamtika
image_query: Royal bridal procession escorted by soldiers through hill jungle
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 106

title: Disaster at Raha and Peace with the Kacharis
body: A strong Ahom garrison was left at Raha under Sundar Gohain, who demanded tribute from the Kacharis. Taking advantage of slackness in the fort, the Kacharis under Bhim Darpa, their king's eldest son, made a night attack in which Sundar was killed. Foreseeing renewed war with the Muhammadans, Pratap Singh sent a peaceful message and presents, and gave the Kachari king a noble's daughter in marriage.
key_facts: Sundar Gohain was killed in a Kachari night attack at Raha
The attack was led by Bhim Darpa, the Kachari king's eldest son
Pratap Singh made peace to prepare for war with the Muhammadans
image_query: Night attack on a bamboo fort by torchlight
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 107

title: Marriage Alliance with the Koch King Parikshit
body: In 1603 Pratap Singh obtained in marriage Mangaldahi, the daughter of the Koch king Parikshit. He gave twenty-three elephants to Parikshit, who sent six families of domestics and twenty female slaves with his daughter. In 1615 Parikshit's brother Bali Narayan, just defeated by the Muhammadans, fled to Pratap Singh for shelter and was received cordially.
key_facts: Pratap Singh married Mangaldahi, daughter of Koch king Parikshit, in 1603
He gave Parikshit twenty-three elephants
Bali Narayan took refuge with the Ahoms in 1615
image_query: Royal wedding gift procession of elephants
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 107

title: The First Mughal Invasion (1615)
body: About 1615 a Muhammadan trader was murdered near Koliabar on suspicion of being a spy, and his two boats were looted. Shekh Qasim, the governor of Bengal, sent Saiad Hakim and Saiad Aba Bakr with upwards of ten thousand horse and foot and four hundred large ships. They were joined by Sattrajit, thanadar of Pandu and Gauhati, and by the Ahom deserter Akhek Gohain.
key_facts: Trigger: murder of a Muslim trader near Koliabar
Sent by Shekh Qasim, governor of Bengal
Over 10,000 men and 400 large ships
Led by Saiad Hakim and Saiad Aba Bakr
image_query: Mughal war fleet sailing up a wide river
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 107

title: Ahom Victory at the Bharali
body: The Mughals won the first battle at the mouth of the Bharali after crossing their horses over the river under cover of fog. A new Ahom commander, advised by Akhek Gohain who had deserted back on a promise of pardon, surprised them with a night attack by land and water and totally defeated them. Saiad Aba Bakr was killed, and Pratap Singh returned in triumph and performed the Rikkhvan ceremony.
key_facts: The Ahoms won by a night attack by land and water
Mughal leader Saiad Aba Bakr was killed
Pratap Singh performed the Rikkhvan ceremony after the victory
image_query: Night river battle with boats and torches
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 108

title: Bali Narayan Becomes Dharma Narayan of Darrang
body: After the victory, Bali Narayan was installed as tributary Raja of Darrang with the title Dharma Narayan. His capital was on the south bank of the Brahmaputra. The pardon promised to Akhek Gohain was later revoked and he was executed, while the Padishahnamah says the disaster led to the removal of Qasim Khan as governor of Bengal.
key_facts: Bali Narayan made tributary Raja of Darrang
He took the title Dharma Narayan
Qasim Khan was removed as governor of Bengal after the defeat
image_query: Tributary king installed in a riverside court
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 108

title: Failed Attack on Hajo (1617–18)
body: In November 1617 Pratap Singh advanced towards Hajo with Dharma Narayan, took Pandu and defeated the Muhammadans at Agiathuti. Against orders to wait, some hot-headed commanders chased a few Muslim horsemen to Hajo and assaulted it. The attack failed; the Ahoms retreated to Srighat, the Burha Gohain was captured, and the officers who had disobeyed were beheaded or starved to death.
key_facts: Advance on Hajo began in November 1617
Ahoms captured Pandu
The unauthorised assault on Hajo failed
The Burha Gohain was taken prisoner
image_query: Hajo hill temple town under siege
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 109

title: Creation of the Bar Phukan and Bar Barua
body: Langi Panisiya, who had rallied the fleeing soldiers, was rewarded with the newly created post of Bar Phukan, governor of the conquered provinces west of Koliabar. The tracts east of Koliabar outside the jurisdiction of the Bar Gohain and Burha Gohain were placed under another new officer, the Bar Barua. The first Bar Barua was Mamai Tamuli, the king's uncle.
key_facts: Both posts were created by Pratap Singh
First Bar Phukan: Langi Panisiya, governing west of Koliabar
First Bar Barua: Mamai Tamuli, the king's uncle, governing east of Koliabar
image_query: Ahom king appointing two officials in court
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 110

title: Victory of 1619 and Submission of the Frontier Chiefs
body: In September 1619 the Muhammadans besieged Dharma Narayan in his fort. An Ahom force faced them for six weeks and then forced a battle in which the Muhammadans were defeated, leaving ten cannon, fifty guns and many weapons behind. Dharma Narayan and frontier chiefs, including those of Dimarua and Hojai, again submitted to Pratap Singh, but the Raja of Koch Bihar rejected his offer of an alliance.
key_facts: Mughals besieged Dharma Narayan in September 1619
Ahoms captured ten cannon and fifty guns
Chiefs of Dimarua and Hojai submitted to Pratap Singh
image_query: Captured cannon lined up after a battle
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 110

title: Sattrajit and the Fall of Langi Bar Phukan
body: Sattrajit, the treacherous thanadar of Pandu, feared a peace between the Mughals and Ahoms and befriended Langi Bar Phukan. When Sattrajit let a conspirator escape to Bengal, Pratap Singh ordered his arrest. The two met on Umananda island opposite Gauhati, embraced, and the Bar Phukan let him go. The king had the Bar Phukan chained in a dungeon and starved to death; Neog succeeded him and the war came to an end.
key_facts: Sattrajit was thanadar of Pandu
The meeting took place on Umananda island opposite Gauhati
Langi Bar Phukan was starved to death for letting Sattrajit go
Neog succeeded him as Bar Phukan
image_query: Umananda island Brahmaputra Guwahati
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 111

title: Causes of the Second War (1635)
body: Relations with the Nawab of Bengal became strained again. The Padishahnamah blames Sattrajit for urging Dharma Narayan to push his boundary into Goalpara when Islam Khan became governor. Pratap Singh also sheltered Harikesh, a defaulting fiscal officer of the Nawab, and refused to surrender him. A force sent in 1635 to seize Harikesh was defeated by the Ahoms near the Bharali river.
key_facts: Islam Khan was the new governor of Bengal
Pratap Singh refused to surrender the fugitive officer Harikesh
A Mughal force was defeated near the Bharali in 1635
image_query: Mughal soldiers crossing a river to seize a fugitive
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 112

title: The Ahoms Carry the War into Kamrup
body: Pratap Singh decided to carry the war into enemy territory. He sent presents to the chiefs of Dimarua, Hojai, Barduar and other frontier tracts, and won over the chiefs of about ten thousand paiks settled by Qasim Khan in Kamrup. His troops took the Muhammadan forts at Deomiha, Bantikot, Chamaria and Nagarbera, and then besieged Hajo, capturing 360 cannon and guns in one battle.
key_facts: Won over chiefs of about 10,000 paiks settled in Kamrup
Captured forts at Deomiha, Bantikot, Chamaria and Nagarbera
Captured 360 cannon and guns in one engagement near Hajo
image_query: Ahom soldiers capturing a mud fort
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 112

title: The First European in Ahom Territory
body: Bengal sent reinforcements to Hajo under Saiad Zainul-abidin, with 210 war sloops and boats. The Buranjis record that a Feringi, or European, serving with the Muhammadans went off alone to shoot birds, was captured and sent to the Ahom king. This is the first recorded instance of a European entering Ahom territory.
key_facts: Reinforcements came under Saiad Zainul-abidin with 210 sloops and boats
A 'Feringi' (European) was captured while shooting birds
First recorded European to enter Ahom territory
image_query: European soldier captured in Assam marshland
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 113

title: Great Ahom Naval Victory
body: When the branch of the Brahmaputra flowing past Hajo dried up, Zainul-abidin joined Abdussalam at Hajo and left the fleet with Muhammad Salih Kambu, Sattrajit and Majlis Bayazid. That night the Ahoms attacked with nearly five hundred ships and won a decisive victory. Muhammad Salih was killed, and the Ahom chroniclers say three hundred boats and three hundred cannon and guns were captured.
key_facts: The Ahoms attacked at night with nearly 500 ships
Mughal commander Muhammad Salih Kambu was killed
About 300 boats and 300 cannon and guns captured
image_query: Night naval battle with hundreds of war boats
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 113

title: Surrender of Hajo
body: Hajo was closely besieged by the Bar Phukan and Dharma Narayan. The starving defenders ate their pack bullocks and camels before Abdussalam agreed to surrender. The leaders were settled at Silpani and given land and slaves, while the common soldiers were distributed as slaves among the Ahom nobles. Zainul-abidin and the rest died trying to break out, and the Muhammadans' brick buildings at Hajo were levelled.
key_facts: Hajo's defenders surrendered after eating their bullocks and camels
Mughal leaders were settled at Silpani
About 2,000 guns and 700 horses were captured
Mughal brick buildings at Hajo were levelled
image_query: Hajo Assam hill temple
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 114

title: The Bar Phukan and the Weavers of Sualkuchi
body: It later came out that the besieged Muhammadan leaders had sent pearls and other valuables to the king through the Bar Phukan, who kept them for himself. He had also taken fifty families of weavers from Sualkuchi and settled them in his own jurisdiction instead of sending them to Upper Assam. For these offences he was arrested and put to death.
key_facts: The Bar Phukan kept pearls meant for the king
He took fifty families of Sualkuchi weavers for himself
He was executed for these offences
image_query: Sualkuchi silk weaver at a traditional loom
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 114

title: Chandra Narayan, Founder of the Bijni Family
body: The remaining Muhammadan garrisons in Kamrup were captured, and in much of Goalpara the Muhammadan yoke was thrown off. Chandra Narayan, a son of the Koch king Parikshit and founder of the Bijni family, established himself at Hatsila in Karaibari on the south bank with Ahom help. Many zamindars on the north bank submitted to the Ahoms.
key_facts: Chandra Narayan was a son of Koch king Parikshit
He founded the Bijni family
Established at Hatsila in Karaibari with Ahom help
image_query: Koch prince establishing a riverside court
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 115

title: Mir Zainuddin and the End of Sattrajit
body: The Nawab of Dacca sent his brother Mir Zainuddin with fifteen hundred horse and four thousand matchlock men. Arriving after Hajo had fallen, he marched against Chandra Narayan, who fled, and the Goalpara zamindars submitted. At Dhubri he found clear proof of Sattrajit's many acts of treachery, arrested him and sent him to Dacca, where he was imprisoned and executed.
key_facts: Mir Zainuddin was the Nawab's brother
Came with 1,500 horse and 4,000 matchlock men
Sattrajit was arrested at Dhubri and executed at Dacca
image_query: Mughal commander arresting a traitor at a river port
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 115

title: Defeat at Jogighopa and Hirapur
body: The Ahoms gathered twelve thousand foot, including Koch allies, and a large fleet. They held Jogighopa on the north bank and Hirapur on the opposite side, with the fleet anchored between the two forts. After several engagements they were defeated, and Chandra Narayan was killed in one of the fights.
key_facts: Ahoms held Jogighopa and Hirapur with 12,000 foot
The fleet was anchored in mid-river between the forts
Chandra Narayan was killed in the fighting
image_query: Two river forts facing each other across the Brahmaputra
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 115

title: The Night Attack of 31 October 1637
body: A Mughal flying column under Muhammad Zaman, Faujdar of Sylhet, entrenched at Bishenpur. The Ahoms, reinforced to forty thousand men, cut off his supplies with palisades and night raids. Receiving twenty thousand more men, they attacked in force on the night of 31 October 1637 and took two stockades, but next morning Muhammad Zaman drove them out, took fifteen of their stockades and killed four thousand Ahoms.
key_facts: Mughal commander: Muhammad Zaman, Faujdar of Sylhet
Ahom night attack on 31 October 1637
The Ahoms lost about four thousand men
image_query: Soldiers storming bamboo stockades at dawn
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 116

title: Disasters at Barepaita and Srighat
body: Three weeks later the united Muhammadan forces attacked the Ahom army at Barepaita from three directions. The Ahoms ran short of ammunition and suffered a crushing defeat. At Srighat a naval battle proved just as disastrous: nearly five hundred sloops and three hundred guns were lost. Alarmed, Pratap Singh prepared to flee to the hills and put his Muhammadan prisoners to death.
key_facts: Crushing Ahom defeat at Barepaita after running out of ammunition
Naval defeat at Srighat: about 500 sloops and 300 guns lost
Koliabar became the rallying point of the Ahom forces
image_query: Defeated war boats burning on a river
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 117

title: Death of Dharma Narayan
body: After the victory the Muhammadans pursued Dharma Narayan, who fled to Singiri Parbat, where he and his two sons were eventually killed. Over the next three months the Muhammadans consolidated their rule in Kamrup and made a financial settlement of the country. Mir Nurullah of Harat was appointed Thanadar with his headquarters at Gauhati.
key_facts: Dharma Narayan and his two sons were killed at Singiri Parbat
The Muhammadans made a revenue settlement of Kamrup
Mir Nurullah became Thanadar at Gauhati
image_query: Lone rocky hill above the Brahmaputra
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 118

title: The Bar Nadi–Asurar Ali Boundary
body: In 1638 a Muhammadan force with Pran Narayan of Koch Bihar was defeated at the mouth of the Bharali and retired to Gauhati. But the long war had exhausted the Ahoms. A treaty fixed the Bar Nadi on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south as the boundary. For the next twenty years the country west of this line remained in Muhammadan hands.
key_facts: Treaty boundary: Bar Nadi (north bank) and Asurar Ali (south bank)
Muhammadans held the land west of it for about twenty years
Traces of their administration survived into Gait's time
image_query: Old raised road through Assam paddy fields
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 118

title: The Kacharis and the Nambar Forest
body: The Kachari king Bhimbal died in 1637 and was succeeded by his son Indra Ballabh, whose friendly letter was coldly received as not respectful enough. From now on messages between the two kingdoms went by Koliabar rather than the old Dhansiri valley route. That valley had been depopulated by the repeated wars and was becoming overgrown with the jungle that now forms the Nambar forest.
key_facts: Kachari king Bhimbal died in 1637
His son Indra Ballabh succeeded him
The war-emptied Dhansiri valley became the Nambar forest
image_query: Nambar forest Assam
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 118

title: Pratap Singh Breaks the Bhuiyas
body: The Bhuiyas, petty chiefs on the north bank between the Bharali and the Subansiri, had stopped paying tribute since the Koch invasion. In 1623 one of them, Uday, declared himself independent and was joined by others. He was captured and executed, and Pratap Singh broke the power of the Bhuiyas for ever by moving them to the south bank and forbidding them to cross to the north bank on any pretext.
key_facts: Bhuiyas held the north bank between the Bharali and the Subansiri
Bhuiya chief Uday rebelled in 1623 and was executed
Bhuiyas were moved to the south bank and forbidden to return
image_query: Villagers crossing a river by boat under guard
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 119

title: Census, Settlers and Embankments
body: Pratap Singh took a census, divided people into clans and appointed officers over them. Four hundred Ahom families were settled around Marangi to guard the Kachari frontier, and artisans were encouraged to immigrate. The towns of Abhaypur and Mathurapur were built, the palace at Garhgaon was protected by an embankment, and the Ladaigarh was constructed as a line of defence.
key_facts: A census was taken and people organised into clans
400 Ahom families settled around Marangi on the Kachari frontier
Towns of Abhaypur and Mathurapur were built
The Ladaigarh embankment was built for defence
image_query: Workers building a long earthen embankment
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 119

title: Death and Legacy of Pratap Singh (1641)
body: Pratap Singh died in 1641 after a reign of 38 years. He was a capable, energetic and ambitious ruler who, despite wars with the Kacharis and Muhammadans, organised his kingdom and built roads, embankments and tanks. He ruled with a firm and heavy hand: even his trusted Bharali Barua was sentenced to death for embezzlement.
key_facts: Pratap Singh died in 1641
He reigned for 38 years
Known for roads, embankments, tanks and strict rule
image_query: Ahom royal funeral procession
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 119

title: The Dopgarh and Frontier Watch
body: The Dopgarh embankment was built against Naga raids, and no Naga could cross it unless accompanied by a peon or kataki. Pratap Singh dropped a plan for an embankment on the Kachari frontier because his nobles said the kingdom was still growing there. Katakis were appointed to watch the Miris and Daflas, and markets and trade flourished between the two great Muhammadan wars.
key_facts: Dopgarh embankment built against Naga raids
Katakis (envoys) watched the Miris and Daflas
A stone bridge was built over the Darika river
image_query: Guarded embankment at the edge of the hills
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 120

title: Gajpati: Lord of a Thousand Elephants
body: Pratap Singh loved elephant hunting and often attended the khedas. His ambition was to own a thousand elephants; when he achieved it, he took the title Gajpati, lord of elephants, and renamed the town of Jamirguri as Gajpur. The Padishahnamah describes him as an infidel who has a thousand elephants and a hundred thousand foot.
key_facts: Pratap Singh owned a thousand elephants
He took the title Gajpati (lord of elephants)
Jamirguri was renamed Gajpur
image_query: Herd of elephants in an Assam grassland
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 120

title: Brahmans and Religion under Pratap Singh
body: The influence of the Brahmans increased considerably. The Somdeo was still worshipped, and the Deodhais still read omens from the legs of fowls before battle. Yet Brahmans consecrated the Misagarh tank, and Siva temples were built at Dergaon and Bishnath with land grants for their upkeep. At the Brahmans' instigation, the Mahapurushias were persecuted and several of their Gosains were put to death.
key_facts: Brahman influence grew under Pratap Singh
Siva temples built at Dergaon and Bishnath
Mahapurushias were persecuted at the Brahmans' instigation
image_query: Biswanath temple Assam
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 121

title: The Ahoms Through Mughal Eyes
body: The Padishahnamah gives a Mughal view of the Ahoms of this time. They shaved their heads and beards. The chiefs rode elephants or ponies, but the army consisted only of foot soldiers, using bows, arrows and matchlocks. Their fleet was large and well fitted out, and they were very brave in naval battles. On the march they quickly fortified their camps with mud walls, bamboo palisades and a ditch.
key_facts: The Ahom army consisted only of foot soldiers
Their fleet was large and they were brave in naval battles
They fortified camps with mud walls, bamboo palisades and a ditch
image_query: Soldiers building a camp with mud walls and bamboo
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 122

title: Surampha, the Bhaga Raja (1641–1644)
body: Pratap Singh's youngest son Sai plotted to seize the throne, but the eldest, Surampha, won over his brother Sutyinpha by promising to make him heir. Surampha became king but broke his word, killed his rivals and even ordered the nobles to furnish sons for burial with his dead adopted son. The exasperated nobles deposed him; he was poisoned in the hills, and is known as the Bhaga (deposed) Raja.
key_facts: Surampha reigned 1641 to 1644
He broke his promise to make Sutyinpha his heir
Deposed by the nobles and later poisoned
Known as the Bhaga Raja
image_query: Plotting nobles in a dim palace room
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 122

title: The Kachari Envoys and the Seal
body: Surampha's reign saw the building of the Salaguri Road. Kachari envoys who came to congratulate him on his accession were expelled in disgrace because their king's letter was sealed with the seal of a Singh, an independent ruler, instead of a Phukan, a subordinate chief. In 1642 a heavy flood drowned many cattle and several earthquakes occurred.
key_facts: The Salaguri Road was built in this reign
Kachari envoys expelled over the seal on their letter
Heavy flood and earthquakes in 1642
image_query: Royal envoy presenting a sealed letter
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 123

title: Sutyinpha, the Nariya Raja (1644–1648)
body: Sutyinpha was called the Nariya (sick) Raja because of his poor health, and Kekora (crooked) because of a curved spine. His installation was celebrated with fights between elephants, between an elephant and a tiger, and between a tiger and a crocodile. Misled by one of his wives, he had his own son by the chief queen treacherously killed, along with the queen's father, the Barpatra Gohain.
key_facts: Sutyinpha reigned 1644 to 1648
Nicknamed Nariya (sick) Raja and Kekora (crooked)
Installation celebrated with animal fights
image_query: Royal arena with an elephant and a tiger
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 123

title: The Dafla Expeditions and the King's Fall
body: An expedition sent against the Daflas in June 1646 failed, and the furious king made its commanders, the Burha Gohain and Barpatra Gohain, appear in public in women's clothes. A second expedition in January 1647 utterly defeated the Daflas and Miris. But the king's cruel son and his own poor health made him unpopular, and in November 1648 the nobles deposed him and made his son Sutamla king.
key_facts: Failed Dafla expedition in June 1646
Daflas and Miris defeated in January 1647
Sutyinpha deposed by the nobles in November 1648
Succeeded by his son Sutamla
image_query: Soldiers marching into forested hills
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 124

title: Jayadhvaj Singh, the Bhagania Raja
body: Sutamla took the Hindu name Jayadhvaj Singh. Because he later fled from Garhgaon during the Muhammadan invasion, he is also known as the Bhagania (fugitive) Raja. At his accession the Somdeo was placed on the throne, guns were fired and gifts were given to the Brahmans. The Raja of Jaintia asked for the return of Dimarua and Kaphanali, but his request was refused.
key_facts: Ahom name Sutamla; Hindu name Jayadhvaj Singh
Reigned 1648 to 1663
Called the Bhagania (fugitive) Raja
image_query: Ahom coronation with drums and a gold throne
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 125

title: Expeditions against the Lakma Nagas and Miris
body: In 1650 and again in 1654 expeditions were sent against the Lakma Nagas for raids. Dafla archers with the Ahom force drove off a Naga spear attack, and eventually the Naga chief submitted and agreed to pay tribute. In 1655 the Miris killed two Ahom subjects; after defeat they agreed to pay a yearly tribute of bison, horses, tortoises, swords and yellow beads, probably amber.
key_facts: Expeditions against the Lakma Nagas in 1650 and 1654
Dafla archers fought alongside the Ahoms
Miris paid tribute including yellow beads, probably amber
image_query: Hill tribe tribute of bison and horses
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 125

title: Jaintia and the Gobha Chief
body: In 1647 the Raja of Jaintia seized an Ahom trader, and Jayadhvaj Singh retaliated by arresting Jaintia traders at Sonapur; all contact stopped for eight years. In 1658 the chief of Gobha, attacked by the Jaintia rebel Pramata Rai, sought Ahom protection with seven hundred men. The Bar Phukan was ordered to establish him in Khagarijan, corresponding roughly to modern Nowgong.
key_facts: Ahom-Jaintia contact was broken for eight years after 1647
The Gobha chief sought Ahom protection in 1658
He was settled in Khagarijan, roughly modern Nowgong
image_query: Hill chief with followers seeking protection
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 126

title: The Ahoms Seize Gauhati (1658)
body: When the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan fell ill in 1658, Pran Narayan of Koch Bihar used the wars of succession to throw off Mughal rule. Jayadhvaj Singh also seized the moment: he built two bridges over the Kallang and marched on Gauhati. The Faujdar fled by boat to Dacca without a fight, and twenty cannon and many horses and guns fell into Ahom hands.
key_facts: Shah Jahan's illness in 1658 set off a war of succession
Jayadhvaj Singh bridged the Kallang and took Gauhati
The Mughal Faujdar fled to Dacca without fighting
image_query: Army crossing a bamboo bridge over a river
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 127

title: Masters of the Whole Brahmaputra Valley
body: Pran Narayan proposed an alliance to divide the Mughal lands in Assam, but the Ahoms, elated by their easy capture of Gauhati, rejected it. They defeated the Koches twice and drove them across the Sankosh, becoming masters of the whole Brahmaputra valley. According to the Alamgirnamah they even plundered the country to the south almost as far as Dacca.
key_facts: The Ahoms rejected Pran Narayan's offer of alliance
They drove the Koches across the Sankosh river
They became masters of the whole Brahmaputra valley
image_query: Victorious army on the bank of a river at sunset
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 128

title: Mir Jumla Sent to Punish Assam
body: When Mir Jumla became governor of Bengal, Aurangzeb told him to punish the lawless zamindars, especially those of Assam and Arakan. Jayadhvaj Singh offered to hand back the imperial lands, but ordered his officers to hold the Jogighopa fort. Mir Jumla occupied Koch Bihar, though its Raja escaped to Bhutan, and on 4 January 1662 set out to invade Assam.
key_facts: Mir Jumla was Aurangzeb's governor of Bengal
He first occupied Koch Bihar
He set out to invade Assam on 4 January 1662
image_query: Mughal general setting out with a great army
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 128

title: The Fall of Jogighopa (1662)
body: Mir Jumla arrived before the Ahom fort at Jogighopa with, according to the Buranjis, twelve thousand horse and thirty thousand foot. The garrison of twelve thousand, weakened by an epidemic, possibly cholera, gave up after a faint-hearted resistance. The fort was guarded by pits full of pointed bamboo spikes, called panjis, which was how the Ahoms fortified all their positions.
key_facts: Mir Jumla's army: about 12,000 horse and 30,000 foot
The Ahom garrison was weakened by an epidemic
Ahom forts were guarded by pits of pointed bamboos (panjis)
image_query: Earthen fort with bamboo spike pits
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 129

title: Mir Jumla's Fleet
body: Mir Jumla's army marched up both banks of the Brahmaputra while his fleet kept pace. The fleet included ghrabs, large vessels carrying about fourteen guns and fifty or sixty men, each towed by four oared boats called kosahs. Most of the ghrabs were commanded by European officers, mostly Portuguese, and there were three to four hundred vessels in all.
key_facts: Ghrabs carried about 14 guns and 50 to 60 men
Each ghrab was towed by four oared kosahs
Many ghrabs had European, mostly Portuguese, officers
image_query: Gun boats towed by rowing boats on a river
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 129

title: Gauhati Falls to Mir Jumla
body: The Ahoms again declined to fight. Their troops on the north bank fled to Kajali, while those on the south bank were overtaken and many were killed. The Srighat fort was demolished, and Gauhati, then mostly on the north bank, was occupied on 4 February 1662. The panic-stricken Ahoms fell back to Samdhara at the mouth of the Bharali and strengthened the forts there and at Simlagarh.
key_facts: Gauhati was occupied on 4 February 1662
Gauhati then lay mostly on the north bank
The Ahoms regrouped at Samdhara and Simlagarh
image_query: Brahmaputra river Guwahati hills
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 130

title: The Storming of Simlagarh
body: The Ahom fort of Simlagarh lay between the Brahmaputra and a range of hills, with thick battlemented walls, trenches and panji pits. Mir Jumla chose a siege rather than a costly assault, pushing covered trenches up to the walls. When the wall was scaled and the gate broken open, the defenders fled, leaving their guns. Mir Jumla was surprised by the strength of the fort, and the garrison of Samdhara fled too.
key_facts: Simlagarh lay between the river and the hills
Taken by siege and a final assault
The Samdhara garrison fled after Simlagarh fell
image_query: Fortress wall between river and hills under siege
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 131

title: Naval Battle above Koliabar
body: Beyond Koliabar the hilly river bank forced Mir Jumla's army inland, leaving his fleet isolated. The Ahoms attacked it with seven or eight hundred ships, and the cannonade lasted all night. At daybreak a relief force arrived, and on hearing its trumpets the Ahoms fled; over three hundred of their ships were captured. Interestingly, the Buranjis, usually frank about reverses, do not mention this defeat.
key_facts: The Ahoms attacked with 700 to 800 ships
The battle lasted all night
Over 300 Ahom ships were captured
The Buranjis do not mention this defeat
image_query: All night cannon battle between river fleets
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 132

title: When the Brahmaputra Ran North of Majuli
body: Lakhau, where the Ahoms tried to make a stand, lay at what was then the meeting point of the Dihing and the Brahmaputra. At that time the Brahmaputra flowed down the course of the present Lohit river, north of Majuli island, while the Dihing followed the present Brahmaputra channel to the south of it. The Ahoms retreated from Lakhau after only a feeble resistance on 9 March 1662.
key_facts: Lakhau lay at the old confluence of the Dihing and Brahmaputra
The Brahmaputra then flowed north of Majuli
The Dihing then followed the present Brahmaputra channel
image_query: Majuli island river channels aerial view
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 133

title: The Flight of Jayadhvaj Singh
body: Jayadhvaj Singh resolved to flee and ordered a thousand boats to carry away his property. He went first to Charaideo and Taraisat, where his council agreed that resistance was impossible. His peace offers were rejected, and he fled on to Tipam and then Namrup, the easternmost province of his kingdom, with some of his nobles and about five thousand men.
key_facts: A thousand boats were collected to carry the king's property
The king fled to Namrup, the easternmost province
About five thousand men went with him
image_query: King fleeing upriver in a fleet of boats
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 133

title: Mir Jumla Enters Garhgaon (17 March 1662)
body: Mir Jumla entered Garhgaon, the Ahom capital, on 17 March 1662 and occupied the king's palace. He found 82 elephants, nearly three lakhs of rupees in gold and silver, and about 170 rice storehouses. During the campaign the Mughals took 675 cannon, one of which threw balls of over two hundred pounds, about 9,000 guns and more than a thousand ships. He is said to have struck coins at Garhgaon in the Emperor's name.
key_facts: Mir Jumla entered Garhgaon on 17 March 1662
675 cannon and over 1,000 ships were captured
Coins were struck at Garhgaon in the Delhi Emperor's name
image_query: Mughal army entering a wooden palace city
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 134

title: The Monsoon Turns the Tide
body: The Mughals camped at Mathurapur and set up outposts around Garhgaon. When the rains came, the Ahoms, though unwilling to risk a pitched battle, cut communications, killed stragglers and harassed the garrisons with night attacks. The garrison of Gajpur was wiped out, and a relief fleet was destroyed. The outposts had to be withdrawn, until only Garhgaon and Mathurapur remained in Mughal hands.
key_facts: The Ahoms fought back with night raids during the rains
The Mughal garrison at Gajpur was destroyed
Only Garhgaon and Mathurapur remained in Mughal hands
image_query: Soldiers in heavy monsoon rain in a flooded camp
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 135

title: Hunger and Disease at Garhgaon
body: Besieged in Garhgaon, the Mughals were attacked day and night. Coarse rice and limes were often the only food; salt sold at thirty rupees a seer. Fever and dysentery raged, and one detachment of fifteen hundred men shrank to five hundred. To add to Mir Jumla's troubles, Pran Narayan returned and drove his garrison out of Koch Bihar.
key_facts: Salt sold at thirty rupees a seer
Fever and dysentery swept the Mughal army
A detachment of 1,500 was reduced to 500
image_query: Sick soldiers in a besieged camp during the rains
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 137

title: The Mughals Recover after the Rains
body: When the rains ended in late September, communications reopened and fresh supplies reached Garhgaon by the end of October. The Mughals recovered their spirit and Jayadhvaj Singh fled again to Namrup. The Ahom commander, the Baduli Phukan, deserted to Mir Jumla. But famine in Bengal cut supplies, Mir Jumla fell seriously ill, and his troops refused to face another rainy season.
key_facts: The rains ended in late September 1662
The Baduli Phukan deserted to the Mughals
Mir Jumla fell seriously ill and his troops were discontented
image_query: Supply boats arriving at a river camp
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 138

title: The Peace Terms of 1663
body: Mir Jumla was forced to accept peace. Jayadhvaj Singh agreed to send a daughter to the imperial harem, to pay 20,000 tolas of gold, 120,000 of silver and 40 elephants at once, and more silver and 90 elephants within a year, with six sons of nobles as hostages. Twenty elephants were to be sent every year, and the land west of the Bharali and the Kallang was ceded to the Emperor.
key_facts: An Ahom princess was sent to the imperial harem
Twenty elephants were to be paid every year
Land west of the Bharali (north bank) and the Kallang (south bank) was ceded
This treaty is often called the Treaty of Ghilajharighat
image_query: Peace treaty signed in a royal tent
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 138

title: Death of Mir Jumla (1663)
body: On 9 January 1663, to the joy of his army, Mir Jumla ordered the return to Bengal. His soldiers were so short of food that for four days they lived on water and their animals on grass. At Kajali, on 7 February 1663, a terrible thunderstorm was followed by an earthquake whose shocks lasted half an hour. Mir Jumla grew worse and died on 30 March 1663, just before his ship reached Dacca.
key_facts: The Mughal army left Assam on 9 January 1663
A great earthquake struck on 7 February 1663
Mir Jumla died on 30 March 1663 near Dacca
image_query: Sick general carried in a palanquin by a river
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 139

title: Jayadhvaj Singh's Last Days
body: After the Mughals left, Jayadhvaj Singh disgraced the officials who had failed in the war and built a stronghold at Namrup. He died in November 1663 after an illness of nine days. He was much influenced by the Brahmans and is said to have become a disciple of Niranjan Bapu, whom he made the first Gosain of the great Auniati Sattra. He also gave land for a Sattra at Jakhalabandha.
key_facts: Jayadhvaj Singh died in November 1663
Niranjan Bapu became the first Gosain of the Auniati Sattra
The king persecuted the Mahapurushia sects
image_query: Auniati Satra Majuli
subject: Assam History
topic: Jayadhvaj Singh and Mir Jumla's Invasion
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 140

title: Shihabuddin's Account of Assam
body: Mir Jumla was accompanied by a writer named Shihabuddin, who wrote a detailed account of the expedition, the people and the country. Gait reproduces it because this contemporary account by a foreign, though critical, observer mentions many things on which the Assamese records are silent. Gait used the translation by Professor Jadunath Sarkar.
key_facts: Shihabuddin accompanied Mir Jumla's invasion
His account describes the Assam of 1662
Gait used Jadunath Sarkar's translation
image_query: Mughal chronicler writing in a tent
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 140

title: Uttarkol and Dakhinkol
body: Shihabuddin describes Assam as about 200 kos long, from Gauhati to Sadiya. The land north of the Brahmaputra was called Uttarkol and the land south of it Dakhinkol. Uttarkol had more people and cultivation, but the kings lived in Dakhinkol because it had more strongholds. From Koliabar to Garhgaon, houses and orchards stretched in an unbroken line along the road.
key_facts: North bank called Uttarkol; south bank Dakhinkol
Assam was about 200 kos from Gauhati to Sadiya
The kings lived in Dakhinkol for its strongholds
image_query: Village road lined with bamboo groves and orchards
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 141

title: Climate, Crops and Salt from Banana Ash
body: Shihabuddin wrote that it rained for eight months of the year. The people were free of diseases like leprosy and goitre then common in Bengal. Rice was the chief crop; wheat, barley and lentils were not grown. Salt was dear, so some people dried and burned banana plants, filtered water through the ashes and used the bitter liquid as a substitute for salt.
key_facts: It rained for about eight months a year
Rice was the chief crop; wheat, barley and lentils were not grown
An alkaline liquid from banana ash was used instead of salt
image_query: Filtering water through banana ash to make a salt substitute
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 142

title: Gold from the River Sand
body: Gold was washed from the sand of the Brahmaputra by ten to twelve thousand people, who each paid the Raja one tola of gold a year. The gold was of low purity, a tola fetching only eight or nine rupees. The currency consisted of cowries, rupees and gold coins stamped with the Raja's stamp; copper coins were not used. Musk, elephants, silver, copper, tin and fragrant aloe wood came from the hills.
key_facts: 10,000 to 12,000 people washed gold from the Brahmaputra
Each paid the Raja one tola of gold a year
Currency: cowries, rupees and gold coins; no copper coins
image_query: Gold washers panning river sand
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 143

title: No Land Tax: Service to the Raja
body: Shihabuddin noted that the Raja took no land tax from cultivators. Instead, in every house one man out of three had to serve the Raja, and any delay in carrying out orders was punished with death, so obedience was complete. He estimated that if Assam were run like the imperial provinces, it could yield forty to forty-five lakhs of rupees in revenue.
key_facts: No land tax was taken from cultivators
One man in three from every house served the Raja
Estimated revenue: 40 to 45 lakhs of rupees under Mughal rule
image_query: Village men reporting for royal service
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 143

title: The Land No Invader Could Hold
body: Shihabuddin wrote that no foreign king had ever conquered Assam. Its kings let no foreigners in and no subjects out, except once a year when a trading party went to the frontier near Gauhati. Invaders were harried by night attacks, found the villages emptied, and were trapped by the rains. He recalls how Husain Shah of Bengal once occupied Assam, but his son and army were surrounded in the rains and destroyed.
key_facts: Assam traded once a year at the frontier near Gauhati
Invaders were defeated by night attacks and the rains
Husain Shah's son and army were destroyed in Assam
image_query: Trading party exchanging goods at a frontier river
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 144

title: The Swargi Raja and His People
body: Jayadhvaj Singh was called the Swargi Raja, from the belief that an ancestor came down from heaven by a golden ladder. Shihabuddin says the people did not eat ghi, spoke a language unlike any in eastern India, and were strong, hardy and warlike. Women did not veil their faces, and people knelt before the Raja with eyes fixed on the ground.
key_facts: The king was called Swargi Raja (heavenly king)
The Ahom kings claimed descent from heaven by a golden ladder
Subjects knelt before the Raja with eyes lowered
image_query: Golden ladder descending from the clouds
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 145

title: Silk, Carving and Everyday Dress
body: People wrapped fine linen round the head, a cloth round the waist and a chaddar on the shoulders; turbans, coats and shoes were not worn. They chewed betel leaf with unripe areca nut. Flowered silk and velvet were excellently woven, and trays, chests, thrones and chairs were carved from single pieces of wood. The Raja and Phukans travelled in carved litters called sinhasans.
key_facts: Fine silks and velvet were woven in Assam
Thrones and chairs were carved from a single piece of wood
The Raja and Phukans rode in litters called sinhasans
image_query: Wooden throne carved from a single log
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 147

title: Boats, Guns and Houses
body: The Ahom war boats, called bacharis, were built strong from heartwood; the Gauhati news-writer once counted 32,000 boats passing that place. Boats of chambal wood would not sink even when swamped. The Ahoms cast excellent matchlocks and artillery and made first-rate gunpowder. Apart from Garhgaon's gates and a few temples, all buildings were of wood, bamboo and straw.
key_facts: Ahom war boats were called bacharis
32,000 boats were once counted passing Gauhati
Ahoms cast excellent matchlocks and cannon
Almost no buildings were of brick or stone
image_query: Long wooden war boats pulled up on a riverbank
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 147

title: The Ahom Army and the Chaudangs
body: Six or seven thousand guards called Chaudangs always guarded the Raja's palace; they were his trusted servants and executioners. Weapons included matchlocks, cannon, arrows, short swords, spears and bows. In war every man had to fight. Shihabuddin believed the real warriors numbered no more than twenty thousand, and noted that they liked to attack on a Tuesday, which they thought auspicious.
key_facts: Chaudangs were the Raja's palace guards and executioners
Every man was liable to fight in war
Tuesday was thought an auspicious day for attacks
image_query: Palace guards with spears at a wooden gate
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 148

title: The Royal Burial Vaults
body: Ordinary people buried their dead with the head to the east. Chiefs built vaults and placed in them the deceased's wives and servants, after killing them, along with gold and silver vessels, cloth and food. The Mughals opened ten vaults and recovered property worth nearly ninety thousand rupees. In one queen's vault, eighty years old, a gold betel box was found with the betel leaf still green.
key_facts: Chiefs were buried in vaults with their wives, servants and valuables
Ten vaults opened by the Mughals yielded about 90,000 rupees
Colonel Dalton later confirmed these finds in Ahom royal mounds
image_query: Charaideo maidams Ahom burial mounds
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 149

title: Garhgaon, the Ahom Capital
body: Garhgaon had four gates of stone set in mud, each joined to the Raja's palace by a high, wide embanked road. Instead of a wall, a bamboo plantation two kos or more wide surrounded the city. Houses stood scattered in the bamboo groves, each with its own orchard and fields, so the city looked like a cluster of villages. Only betel sellers traded in the bazaar, since every household stored a year's food.
key_facts: Garhgaon had four stone gates
A belt of bamboo two kos wide served as its wall
Families stored a whole year's food at home
image_query: Old Ahom capital surrounded by bamboo groves
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 149

title: The Royal Audience Hall
body: The Raja's audience hall, the solang, was 120 cubits long and 30 wide, resting on 66 smooth pillars each four cubits round. Its carved wooden lattices and polished brass mirrors dazzled the eye in sunlight, and Shihabuddin thought no one in the world could build and carve wooden houses like the Assamese. It took 12,000 men a year to build. Houses were raised on wooden platforms because of the damp.
key_facts: The audience hall (solang) was 120 cubits long and stood on 66 pillars
Decorated with carved lattices and brass mirrors
Built by 12,000 men in one year
image_query: Great carved wooden audience hall with brass mirrors
subject: Assam History
topic: Assam in 1662: A Mughal Observer's Account
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 150

title: Chakradhvaj Singh Takes the Throne (1663)
body: Jayadhvaj Singh left no sons, so the nobles placed the Saring Raja on the throne. The Deodhais named him Supungmung, and he took the Hindu name Chakradhvaj Singh. The Brahmans and Ganaks were feasted at his installation. The Koch Raja of Darrang, who had sided with Mir Jumla, sent congratulations, and friendly relations were restored.
key_facts: Jayadhvaj Singh left no sons
The Saring Raja became king as Supungmung
His Hindu name was Chakradhvaj Singh
image_query: New king crowned in a wooden palace
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 151

title: Refusing to Pay the Indemnity
body: Mughal officials came to remind the new king that the indemnity was overdue. Chakradhvaj complained that the Mughals had broken faith over the boundary and had not released the prisoners of war. Even after Aurangzeb promised to give up land that had never belonged to the Koch kings, he still withheld payment, saying the treasury was empty and the elephants were not yet trained.
key_facts: Chakradhvaj withheld the rest of the war indemnity
He accused the Mughals of breaking faith on the boundary and prisoners
Excuses: an empty treasury and untrained elephants
image_query: Envoy refused at a royal court
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 152

title: The Great Drought of 1665
body: The year 1665 saw an exceptionally severe drought that stopped cultivation and forced people in many places to dig deep wells for drinking water. Gait notes that this is the only occasion in the whole course of Assam's history when the rains failed badly enough to cause a complete failure of the crops. In the same year the Ahoms subdued the Banchang Nagas and the Miris.
key_facts: Severe drought in 1665
Deep wells were dug for drinking water
The only recorded complete crop failure from drought in Assam's history
image_query: Cracked dry paddy field under a harsh sun
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 153

title: Chakradhvaj Decides to Fight (1667)
body: Early in 1667 Firuz Khan, Thanadar of Gauhati, demanded the unpaid balance of the indemnity, about Rs. 1,12,000 with elephants valued at Rs. 2,000 each. Chakradhvaj had already repaired his forts and army, and despite his nobles' warnings he chose war. In August 1667, after sacrifices to Indra, an army set out to take Gauhati under Rachit, son of the Bar Barua, who was made Bar Phukan.
key_facts: Firuz Khan demanded about Rs. 1,12,000 still due
The Ahom army set out in August 1667
Commander: Rachit (Lachit), son of the Bar Barua, made Bar Phukan
image_query: Ahom general leading an army out at dawn
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 153

title: The Recovery of Gauhati (1667)
body: The Ahoms took the Mughal outposts at Kajali and Bansbari at the first assault and built forts at Kajali and Latasil. Gauhati and Pandu were captured after a two-month siege. In November Mughal reinforcements arrived by warship but were driven back to the Manas river, where they were surrounded and destroyed. The captured officers were sent to Garhgaon.
key_facts: Outposts at Kajali and Bansbari fell at the first assault
Gauhati and Pandu captured after a two-month siege
Mughal relief force destroyed at the Manas river
image_query: Army retaking a riverside hill town
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 154

title: Inscriptions of Victory
body: An Assamese inscription on the Kanai Barasi rock in Kamrup records an Ahom fort built there in Saka 1589 (1667 A.D.) after the defeat and death of Saiad Firuz. A cannon at Silghat bears a Sanskrit inscription praising Chakradhvaj Singh for destroying the Muhammadans in 1589 Saka. A cannon at Dikom bears a similar inscription and also a Persian one dated 1074 Hijri (1663 A.D.).
key_facts: Kanai Barasi rock inscription dated Saka 1589 (1667 A.D.)
Silghat cannon inscription praises Chakradhvaj Singh
Dikom cannon carries a Persian inscription of 1663
image_query: Ancient rock inscription Guwahati
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 154

title: Aurangzeb Sends Raja Ram Singh
body: The news of Gauhati's loss reached Aurangzeb in December 1667, and he sent Raja Ram Singh with 18,000 cavalry, 30,000 infantry and 15,000 archers from Koch Bihar. He reached Rangamati in February 1669 and demanded the old Bar Nadi–Asurar Ali boundary. The Bar Phukan replied that he would rather fight than yield an inch of territory. Meanwhile Gauhati had become the Bar Phukan's headquarters.
key_facts: Raja Ram Singh was sent by Aurangzeb
His army: 18,000 cavalry, 30,000 infantry and 15,000 archers
He reached Rangamati in February 1669
Gauhati became the Bar Phukan's headquarters
image_query: Mughal Rajput commander leading a great army
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 155

title: Ram Singh's Campaign and a Royal Challenge
body: The Ahoms lost two battles near Tezpur in April 1669 but won a naval battle and repulsed an attack on their fort at Rangmahal. Ram Singh quarrelled with Rashid Khan, cutting his tent ropes and ordering him out of the camp. Ram Singh is said to have challenged Chakradhvaj Singh to single combat, but the Ahom king declined. After further fighting both sides grew tired, and hostilities were suspended.
key_facts: Battles near Tezpur in April 1669
Ram Singh expelled Rashid Khan from his camp
Ram Singh challenged the Ahom king to single combat
image_query: Two armies facing each other across a river
subject: Assam History
source: Gait, A History of Assam (1926), p. 156

title: Udayaditya Singh Comes to the Throne
body: Soon afterwards Chakradhvaj Singh died. His reign was so full of wars that the only new road built was from Teliadanga to Jhanzimukh. His brother Maju Gohain succeeded him as Sunyatpha, taking the Hindu name Udayaditya Singh and marrying his late brother's wife. Negotiations with Ram Singh continued.

title: The Final Defeat of Ram Singh (1671)
body: Ram Singh advanced to Sitamari while talks were going on, so Udayaditya renewed the war. After a hard struggle the arrival of the Bar Phukan with more ships let the Ahoms defeat the Mughal navy and win on land as well. Helped by the Garos and the Raja of Rani, the Ahoms wore Ram Singh down, and in March 1671 he retreated to Rangamati. This final campaign is remembered today as the Battle of Saraighat.

title: The New Western Frontier
body: Udayaditya received the news of Ram Singh's retreat with great joy and loaded the Bar Phukan with presents. Hadira, opposite Goalpara, became the Ahom frontier outpost. Chandra Narayan, grandson of Bali Narayan, was installed as tributary Raja of Darrang, and Gandharba Narayan as Raja of Beltola. The Muhammadans showed no wish to renew the war, and there were some years of peace.

title: The Failed Dafla Expedition
body: A thousand men under the Bar Barua were sent against the Daflas, who had refused tribute, killed three men and carried off forty women and children. The Daflas hid in the jungle and later destroyed the Ahom advance guard in a hill village. When the Bar Barua retreated, the king ordered him to be stripped and put to death, but the queen-mother's plea reduced the sentence to dismissal and banishment.

title: Chakrapani and the Murder of Udayaditya (1673)
body: Udayaditya was so impressed by the learning of Chakrapani, a Vaishnava priest descended from Sankar Deb, that he made him his spiritual guide. Offended nobles persuaded the king's younger brother to rebel. He broke down a city gate at night and seized the king, who was poisoned at Charaideo in August 1673. His three wives were killed, and the priest was impaled and set adrift on a raft on the Dikhu.

title: Legacy of Udayaditya: Ahom-Made Cannon
body: Udayaditya's reign was remarkable chiefly for driving the Musalmans out of Kamrup and fortifying Gauhati. By now the Ahoms could make their own cannon: one at Gauhati bears an inscription saying it was made by order of the Sola Dhara Barua in Saka 1594, or 1672 A.D. In 1671 a treasure house burned down through the Bharali Barua's carelessness with a lit pipe.
